Timeline depends heavily on your business type and district. A standard office can be approved in as little as 15 days.
Expect 45–90 days if you're opening a restaurant or cafe. Retail and service businesses are usually 15–30 days.
The slowest part is municipal inspections, which can add 2–4 weeks. What type of business are you opening?
alcohol: An alcohol licence (TAPDK Belgesi) is issued by the Ministry of Agriculture and takes 4–8 weeks on its own.
You'll need both a TAPDK licence and a Canlı Müzik İzni if you want music. Want me to include those in your roadmap?
TAPDK approval is separate from your main business permit and adds significant time. Plan for 6–12 weeks total.
Selling alcohol requires a TAPDK Belgesi — this is non-negotiable and must be displayed at your premises.
Alcohol licensing in Turkey is handled federally. Even if your municipality approves everything else, you still need TAPDK separately.
music: Live music requires a Canlı Müzik İzni from your district municipality. It's applied for separately from your general business permit.
For recorded background music you may not need a special permit, but live performances always require a Canlı Müzik İzni.
The live music permit is tied to your specific venue address. Moving locations means reapplying.
Canlı Müzik İzni approval typically takes 2–4 weeks from the municipality. Want to start that process?
Some districts have noise ordinances that affect late-night live music. Which district are you in?
steps: There are 14 key legal steps to open a business in Istanbul: Tax ID, legal type, company name, NACE code, articles of association, address, notarization, capital deposit, trade registry, bank account, tax office, municipal forms, accountant, and launch. Want details on any step?
The 14-step process starts with your Tax ID and ends with your operating permit. Which step are you on?
Want me to generate the full 14-step roadmap tailored to your business type and district?
The critical steps are Tax ID, Trade Registry, and Municipal Permit. Everything else builds on those three.
Step 1 is always the Tax ID (Vergi Numarası). Have you done that yet?
cafe: A cafe has the same fire compliance requirements as a restaurant — you need an İtfaiye report and Baca certificate even without a full kitchen. Want the checklist?
Cafes serving pastries or light food fall under municipal hygiene rules. Expect 30–60 days for full approval.
If your cafe serves alcohol, a TAPDK Belgesi is mandatory regardless of size. Want that included in your roadmap?
For a small cafe without a full kitchen the process is faster — usually 30–45 days. What district are you in?
Cafes also need a Gıda Sicil Belgesi (Food Registry) from the municipality. Want to see the full document list?
clothing: Clothing stores need an İşyeri Açma ve Çalışma Ruhsatı from the district municipality. Fire requirements are less strict than F&B businesses.
A clothing store permit is one of the simpler ones — expect 15–30 days once your Trade Registry and NACE code are in order.
Retail clothing shops don't need an İtfaiye report unless the space exceeds a certain size threshold. What's your store's approximate m²?
For a clothing store, your NACE code will be 4771 (Retail sale of clothing). Want me to walk through the documents needed?
Retail permits are primarily handled at the district municipality. Trade registry and tax registration are prerequisites. Want the full checklist?
retail: Retail businesses in Istanbul need an İşyeri Açma ve Çalışma Ruhsatı — the process is straightforward and usually takes 15–30 days.
General retail doesn't trigger the İtfaiye inspection unless you stock flammable materials or exceed the size threshold. What type of products are you selling?
For any retail operation you'll need: Tax ID, Trade Registry, NACE code, signed lease, and the municipal operating licence. Want to dig into any of these?
Retail permits in Istanbul are handled at your district belediye. Which district are you planning to open in?
Your NACE code is the most important classification for retail permits — it determines your tax and regulatory obligations. Do you know your product category?
office: Office and consultancy businesses have the simplest permit requirements in Istanbul — mainly the İşyeri Açma Ruhsatı and basic tax registration. Expect 10–20 days.
An office permit doesn't need an İtfaiye report in most cases. Your main requirements are Trade Registry, NACE code, lease, and municipal licence.
For a service-based office (consulting, tech, marketing), the NACE code determines your classification. Want help picking the right one?
Office permits are the fastest to get — usually 2 weeks. The limiting factor is Trade Registry processing time.
Co-working spaces used as a registered address may require a 'sanal ofis' agreement. Is this for a physical desk or just a registered address?
barber: A barber shop (berber) needs an İşyeri Açma Ruhsatı plus a GSM (Gayresiħhî Müessese) certificate for personal hygiene businesses in Istanbul.
For a barber or hair salon, you’ll also need proof that the owner or manager holds a professional berber certificate (kalfalık/ustalık belgesi).
Barbershops fall under the 'personal care services' category — NACE code 9602. This affects your municipal inspections.
The  certificate for a barber shop involves a municipal hygiene inspection. Expect 2–4 weeks for that alone.
Hair salons and barbershops must display their professional certificate and İşyeri Ruhsatı visibly at the premises. Want the full checklist?
gym: A gym or fitness center needs an İşyeri Açma Ruhsatı plus a Spor Salonu compliance check from the local Sports Directorate (Gençlik ve Spor İl Müdürlüğü).
Gyms over a certain m² may require a fire safety (İtfaiye) inspection. What's the planned size of your facility?
For a gym, you’ll need at least one certified sports trainer on staff before the licence is issued.
NACE code for gyms and fitness centers is 9311 or 9312. This affects your insurance and regulatory requirements.
Fitness centers in Istanbul must also register with the Ministry of Youth and Sports — this runs parallel to the municipal permit.
pharmacy: Opening a pharmacy (eczane) requires approval from the Turkish Pharmacists Association (TEB) in addition to the standard municipal permit.
Pharmacy licences are regulated at the provincial level — the İl Sağlık Müdürlüğü (Provincial Health Directorate) is your primary contact.
There are strict geographical quotas for pharmacies in Turkey — you can only open one within defined population ratios per district.
A pharmacist's licence (eczacı ruhsatnamesi) is mandatory and must be displayed. The municipality permit comes after TEB approval.
The pharmacy permit process involves TEB, Provincial Health Directorate, and the district municipality — plan for 3–6 months in total.
bakery: A bakery (fırın) needs an İşyeri Açma Ruhsatı, a Gıda Sicil Belgesi, and a Baca Uygunluğu certificate for the chimney/oven flue.
Bakeries with production kitchens are subject to the same hygiene inspections as restaurants — expect 30–60 days.
For a retail bakery selling pre-made items with no on-site baking, the requirements are similar to a standard food retail store.
The chimney/flue compliance (Baca Uygunluğu) is a key step for bakeries — inspected by both the municipality and fire department.
Bakeries producing bread for wholesale also need an İl Gıda ve Tarım Müdürlüğü registration. Is this for retail or wholesale production?
cost: Permit fees in Istanbul vary by business type — a simple retail permit usually runs 500–2,000 TL in municipal fees, while restaurant permits (fire + hygiene inspections included) can reach 5,000–10,000 TL total. What type of business are you opening?

Great question to ask upfront! The main costs are: Trade Registry fee (~500–1,500 TL), notary fees (~500–2,000 TL), and the municipal permit fee (500–5,000 TL depending on business type). For food businesses, add inspection fees on top. Want a breakdown?

The total cost depends on your business type. Offices are cheapest (1,500–3,000 TL all-in), retail is mid-range (2,000–5,000 TL), and food businesses are the most expensive due to fire and hygiene inspections (5,000–15,000 TL). What are you opening?

Beyond the permit fees, don’t forget accountant setup costs (~500–1,500 TL/month ongoing) and notary fees for your Articles of Association. The government fees alone are usually 2,000–8,000 TL depending on your business. Want the full cost breakdown?

The İşyeri Açma ve Çalışma Ruhsatı is handled at your local district municipality. Most applications can now be started via turkiye.gov.tr, but inspections usually require an in-person visit. Which district are you in?

Your district belediye is your main contact for operating permits — they handle the İşyeri Açma Ruhsatı, hygiene inspections, and the municipal side of fire clearance. Where in Istanbul is your business going to be?

Different districts in Istanbul can have slightly different processing speeds. Kadıköy, Beşiktaş, Sisli, and Bakırköy tend to be well-organised for international applicants. Which area are you looking at?

For most permits, you submit to your district municipality either via e-Devlet or in person. The Trade Registry and Tax Office are separate stops. Want me to walk you through where to go for each step?
how_it_works: Great place to start! Opening a business in Istanbul involves three pillars: ① Company registration (Tax ID, Trade Registry, MERSİS), ② Operating licence (district municipality), ③ Sector-specific licences (fire, hygiene, TAPDK, etc. depending on your business). Want the full step-by-step?

Here’s the big picture: register your company first (Tax ID → MERSİS → Notary → Trade Registry → Bank Account → Tax Office), then apply for your operating licence at the district municipality. The whole process takes 15–90 days depending on your business type. What are you planning to open?

Think of it as 3 phases: ① Company setup (1–2 weeks), ② Operating permit application (1–3 weeks), ③ Sector inspections if required (2–6 weeks for food businesses). It’s bureaucratic but very manageable once you know the path. Want your personalised roadmap?

Every business needs a base set of permits (Tax registration, Trade Registry, municipal operating licence). On top of that, food businesses need hygiene and fire clearance, alcohol sellers need TAPDK, and so on. Tell me your business type and I’ll map out exactly what applies to you!

The system has two tracks: the company registration track (through MERSİS and the Trade Registry) and the premises permit track (through your district municipality). Both must be completed before you can open. Want me to walk you through both from start to finish?
nace: Your NACE code is your official business activity classification in Turkey — it determines your tax category, permit tier, and which inspections apply to you. What type of business are you opening? I can help you find the right code.

NACE codes in Turkey follow the European standard. Common ones: 56.10 (Restaurant), 47.11 (Grocery/Supermarket), 62.01 (Software), 96.02 (Hair Salon), 47.71 (Clothing Retail). What’s your business activity?

You select your NACE code inside the MERSİS portal during registration — it’s the 'Faaliyet Ekle' (Add Activity) button. The code you choose affects your tax obligations and which municipal inspections you’ll need. Want help picking the right one?
Getting your NACE code right is important — an incorrect code can cause problems with permits and tax filings later. Tell me your business type and I’ll point you to the exact code you need.

The NACE code is added during the MERSİS application (step 4 of company formation). Common mistake: choosing too broad a code — always pick the most specific one that matches your actual activity. Want me to find yours?
tax_id: Your Tax ID (Vergi Kimlik Numarası) is the very first step for any foreign national opening a business in Turkey. You get it at your local tax office (Vergi Dairesi) with your passport. It’s free and usually takes about 30 minutes!
To get a Turkish Tax ID, visit your nearest Vergi Dairesi with your passport. Some offices also let you apply online via ivd.gib.gov.tr if you have a Turkish e-Devlet ID. Which city are you in?

The Tax ID (Vergi Numarası) is step one — you can’t open a bank account, register a company, or apply for most permits without it. The good news: it’s quick, free, and just needs your passport. Go to any local tax office.

Got your Tax ID already? Excellent — that’s the foundation for everything else. Next you’ll decide on your company structure (Ltd. or Sole Proprietorship) and then reserve your company name in MERSİS.

Turkish citizens use their national ID number as their Tax ID automatically. Foreign nationals must visit a Vergi Dairesi in person with their passport. The whole thing takes under an hour and costs nothing — one of the easiest steps in the whole process!

residence_permit: As a student in Turkey you need a Student Residence Permit (ikamet) within 30 days of arriving. Have you started the application on the Göç İdaresi portal?

company_formation: Forming a company in Turkey? Great decision. The most common choice for foreigners is an Ltd. Şirket (LLC) — it needs just 10,000 TL in share capital and one director. Want me to walk you through all the steps right from MERSİS registration?
Setting up a Limited Şirket in Turkey takes about 5–10 business days if your documents are lined up. Before we start — do you have all shareholders' IDs and a registered office address ready?
Turkey is actually quite business-friendly for company formation. The MERSİS portal handles name reservation and article generation online. Ready for the full step-by-step walkthrough?

For most foreign entrepreneurs in Turkey, an Ltd. Şirket is the way to go — flexible structure, no maximum shareholder cap, and low minimum capital. Shall I generate your complete company formation roadmap?

The fastest way to get started is to reserve your company name through the MERSİS portal. Once that's confirmed, we can move to notarization and Trade Registry — usually done within a week. Want the full breakdown?
contract_review: Happy to help you review that contract. Could you tell me what type it is — employment, lease, service agreement, or an NDA? That'll let me flag the most relevant risk areas for you.

Contract issues in Turkey are covered by the Turkish Code of Obligations. The most common problem areas are penalty clauses, termination conditions, and jurisdiction. Which part is giving you trouble?
Before signing anything, it's always worth having a lawyer check for one-sided terms. Tell me what the contract is about and I'll walk you through the key things to watch out for.

I can help you flag risky clauses. Under Turkish law, certain types of contracts — real estate, shareholder agreements, power of attorney — also require notarization to be enforceable. What kind of contract are we looking at?
Spotted something off in your contract? Smart move to check before signing. Share the key clauses you're worried about and I'll explain your rights and options under Turkish law.
employment_law: That sounds like a serious situation — and you're right to look into your rights. Under Turkish Labour Law No. 4857, employees who've worked for over a year are entitled to both notice pay and severance. Has your employer given you a written termination notice?

Unfair dismissal claims in Turkey must be filed within 1 month of termination — so timing really matters here. Has the dismissal already happened, or are you still employed and dealing with an ongoing issue?

Employment disputes in Turkey typically start with mandatory mediation (arabuluculuk) before any court action. Most cases are resolved there in 2–3 sessions, which saves months. Want to understand the full process?

Turkish labour courts are generally employee-friendly, and the burden of proof sits with the employer. Let's start by calculating what you're entitled to — severance, unused leave, and notice pay. Can you share how long you've been employed?

Severance pay (kıdem tazminatı) is calculated as 30 days' salary for every year of service. If you were let go without cause, you're likely owed more than just that. Want me to map out everything you can claim?
residence_permit: Work permits in Turkey must be applied for by your employer through the Ministry of Labour's portal — you can't apply on your own. Has your employer already started the process, or do they need guidance on how to proceed?

For a residence permit (ikamet), you apply online at e-ikamet.goc.gov.tr before your current visa or entry stamp expires. The key documents are your passport, health insurance, biometric photos, and a notarized address document. Shall I walk you through each step?

The work permit process takes 4–8 weeks from submission. The good news is your employer handles most of the paperwork — you mainly provide your passport, ID, and insurance. Want the full step-by-step guide?

Applying for a residence permit? Book your appointment on e-ikamet.goc.gov.tr as soon as possible — slots in big cities fill up fast. You'll need health insurance and a notarized rental agreement ready before the appointment.
If your work permit is approved, a residence permit is automatically granted alongside it. But health insurance coverage must be active from day one. Is your insurance policy already in place?
dispute: Legal disputes in Turkey usually follow this path: formal written notice (ihtarname) → mandatory mediation → court, if needed. Most commercial disputes are resolved at mediation and never reach court. What type of dispute are you dealing with?

Before filing any lawsuit in Turkey, your lawyer sends a notarized warning letter (ihtarname) to the other party. This is both a legal requirement for some cases and a smart negotiation move. Would you like help understanding that process?

Turkish commercial law requires mandatory mediation before court for most business disputes. It's confidential, usually done in 3 sessions, and saves months of litigation. Has a mediator been contacted yet?

Court proceedings in Turkey are conducted in Turkish, and your lawyer handles all communications. The key is getting your evidence documented thoroughly before filing. What evidence do you have available right now?

If the court rules in your favour and the other party still doesn't pay, your lawyer can initiate enforcement proceedings (icra takibi) to seize assets. It's a powerful tool — but let's try mediation first. What's the nature of the dispute?
